summary: Spec-Agent infers per-function pre/postconditions for large C++ codebases. It picks a target logic (propositional, first-order, separation logic, or FO separation logic) from Tree-sitter features and heap tracing, has an LLM propose a contract, compiles it to runtime assertions, and validates it with libFuzzer harnesses lifted from existing unit tests, feeding counterexamples back with gains plateauing by ~20 attempts (Fig. 6). On 651 BDE and 508 BlazingMQ functions it reports 85.87% / 77.73% fuzz-valid contracts with open models, versus 81.48% / 66.69% for Claude Code with Opus 4.6.

claims.claim: Spec-Agent synthesizes valid specifications for ~85% of target functions.
claims.evidence: Table 1: BDE 81.00-85.87% Test Valid across four open models; BMQ 69.77-77.73%. The abstract's '85%' is the best BDE figure. 'Valid' includes trivial contracts (5.6-17.1% reduce to true).

claims.claim: No false positives under fuzzing and expert validation.
claims.evidence: Fuzz-passing is the acceptance criterion, so 0% 'Test Invalid' is partly by construction. Independent check is two experts reviewing a random 100 specs per repo plus all harnesses (§4 setup, App. D); no inter-rater statistic beyond 'both agreed'.

claims.claim: Outperforms Claude Code Opus 4.6 at 10x lower token cost.
claims.evidence: App. B Table 5 (BDE): token volumes are similar (Opus 3.3M in / 2.2M out vs Qwen3-Coder-Next 3.2M / 1.0M). The ~10x is dollar cost ($41.0 vs $4.0) from Anthropic list price vs Together AI open-model price, not token count. The accuracy edge on BDE is 4.4pt (85.87 vs 81.48).

claims.claim: Fuzzing adds validation value beyond unit tests.
claims.evidence: Table 3: fuzzer rejects 0.4% (BDE) and 8.0% (BMQ) of contracts that already passed unit tests.

claims.claim: Spec-Agent produces more expressive contracts (more FOL/SL).
claims.evidence: Table 2 counts and Avg. Atoms 3.35/4.15 vs 2.34/2.46 for Opus (Table 1).

patterns.note: Formal contracts (separation logic) validated dynamically; fuzzing as pseudo-oracle, not proof.
Counterexample-guided refinement loop with executable validation; Fig. 6 shows gains plateau by ~20 attempts.
Infers specs from code (reverse direction) rather than spec-first development; contracts could seed specs for legacy code.
Static (Tree-sitter) + dynamic (heap trace) analysis selects target logic deterministically before the LLM call.
Authors attribute the win over Claude Code subagents to a deterministic single-call-per-attempt loop vs exploratory subagents under the same budget (§4); this is plausible but not ablated.
Claude Code's subagent exploration consumed budget with lower validity on this narrow task (Table 1); evidence is indirect.
Reuses existing unit tests as fuzz-harness seeds; tests are held out from generation.

methodology.sample: 1,159 documented, unit-tested public functions (651 BDE, 508 BlazingMQ) from two C++ repos totaling >4M LOC; 100 random specs per repo expert-reviewed.
methodology.baselines: Claude Code (Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.6) with same prompts, tests and harnesses and a 6M weighted-token budget; prior spec-synthesis tools only compared qualitatively (Table 4), including authors' own Fun2Spec.
methodology.variance: Greedy decoding, single run; no seeds or CIs; Claude Code runs (non-deterministic) appear to be single runs.
methodology.ablations: Attempts-vs-validity curve (Fig. 6) and fuzz rejection rates (Table 3); no ablation of language selector or of counterexample feedback.
methodology.contamination_controls: None discussed; BDE and BlazingMQ are public GitHub repos likely in pretraining data.

standards.artifacts: No code or data link found in the paper; builds on authors' Fun2Spec (FSE'26 industry track).

biases.detail: '10x lower token cost' is dollar pricing (Anthropic vs Together AI), not tokens; token counts are within ~1.3x (App. B Table 5).
Validity is judged by the system's own fuzz pseudo-oracle, which also gates acceptance; 0% invalid is partly tautological.
No code, prompts or synthesized contracts released.
Evaluated repos are long-public open source; no contamination discussion.
Single greedy runs; Claude Code baseline single run.

Two repositories selected for strong docs and tests; BDE is Bloomberg's own library (ref [2]: github.com/bloomberg/bde), i.e. the authors' organization. The paper does not state BlazingMQ's provenance.

coi.affiliations: All three authors at Bloomberg, NY.
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Evaluates own system on BDE (Bloomberg's open-source library per ref [2]) and BlazingMQ; compares against Anthropic's Claude Code, a competitor tool, not their product.
coi.detail: Bloomberg is not an AI tooling vendor and Spec-Agent is not marketed. Authors grading their own system (built on their own Fun2Spec) on a codebase from their organization is self-evaluation rather than commercial COI.

verdict_reason: Interesting, well-engineered generate-validate-refine loop with real codebases. However, the headline cost claim is a pricing artifact, 'no false positives' rests largely on the acceptance oracle itself, there is no variance and no artifacts, and it covers two C++ repos from the authors' organization.
applicability: The method does not transfer directly to a Java team (C++/libFuzzer/separation logic). The architecture does transfer: deterministic analysis picks the spec form, an LLM proposes, and an executable oracle built from existing unit tests (for Java: Jazzer or jqwik property tests, or JML/OpenJML assertions) rejects candidates, with counterexamples fed back. This is a concrete template for back-filling machine-checkable contracts on legacy ingestion/delivery code before spec-driven development. Contracts at repo boundaries (DTO invariants, content-schema preconditions) could serve as cross-repo specs. It is evidence that a tight deterministic loop with a cheap open model can match a frontier agent host on a narrow verification task, which supports the 'qr verifies' stance. It is not evidence that open models are 10x cheaper in tokens.
